title: Torsion balances as operational probes of semiclassical gravity: Matched-filter bounds, torque-diffusion constraints, and quantum-noise benchmarks
abstract: Calibrated torsion-balance spectra constrain deterministic and stochastic deviations from standard Newtonian gravity. Using one-sided spectra, we derive a calibrated angle-equivalent noise budget and finite-time matched-filter/Cramér-Rao bounds for known torque templates. For stochastic models, subtracting the calibrated standard noise budget (thermal, Newtonian, environmental, imprecision, backaction) from the observed angle spectrum yields a residual spectrum, convertible to an equivalent residual torque spectrum via calibrated torsional susceptibility. This bounds additional stationary stochastic torque noise. This frequency-resolved bound compresses to a single torque-diffusion coefficient, $D_τ$, only in the Markovian white-noise limit; non-Markovian or colored models require the full residual spectrum. Page--Geilker branch discrimination and Fedida-Kent mixture-equivalence tests address distinct physical questions, but upon projection onto torque templates, both reduce to the same statistical matched-filter discrimination problem. For a room-temperature Cavendish benchmark, resonant thermal angle ASD is $1.36\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{rad}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, while measurement-added SQL is $3.25\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{rad}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. For the Yan \emph{et al.} search, the reported $0.3\,μ\mathrm{rad}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ sensitivity at $2.5\,\mathrm{mHz}$ yields a conservative bound $D_τ\lesssim 2.4\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{N^2\,m^2\,s}$, assuming white torque noise. These formulations provide an interface linking calibrated torsion-balance data, deterministic tests, and stochastic semiclassical-gravity searches, without asserting a direct test of the full relativistic semiclassical Einstein equation.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive statistical framework for analyzing torsion-balance data to test deviations from Newtonian gravity. It quantifies constraints on both deterministic signals and stochastic noise sources by carefully subtracting calibrated noise budgets. The methodology provides a standardized, quantum-limited interface for experimental searches in semiclassical gravity.
main_problem: The paper aims to use calibrated torsion-balance measurements to set rigorous bounds on both deterministic and stochastic deviations from standard Newtonian gravity, providing an interface for testing semiclassical gravity models.
main_result: The analysis derives specific bounds, such as a torque-diffusion coefficient $D_τ \lesssim 2.4	imes10^{-23}\,\mathrm{N^2\,m^2\,s}$ from existing sensitivities, which constrain potential deviations from standard gravity.
method: It employs advanced signal processing techniques, including matched-filter bounds (Cramér-Rao) for deterministic signals and residual spectrum analysis for stochastic noise, all calibrated against known noise sources.
model_or_system: The physical system is a torsion balance, modeled as a linear torsional oscillator. The analysis incorporates the full noise budget, including thermal, Newtonian, environmental, imprecision, and backaction noise sources, using the torsional susceptibility $\chi(\omega)$.
key_observables: Calibrated angle-equivalent noise budget, residual torque spectrum, and the torque-diffusion coefficient ($D_τ$).
important_parameters: Room-temperature resonant thermal ASD ($1.36	imes10^{-4}\,\mathrm{rad}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$) and the measurement-added SQL ($3.25	imes10^{-12}\,\mathrm{rad}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis constrains observable torque projections rather than testing the full relativistic semiclassical Einstein equation, and the white-noise limit is required to simplify the stochastic bound to $D_τ$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a standardized measurement interface using one-sided PSDs, details the matched-filter formalism for deterministic tests, and develops the residual spectrum analysis for stochastic noise, culminating in the derivation of $D_τ$.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of quantum noise analysis (e.g., backaction, quantum limits) to macroscopic, low-frequency gravitational measurements provides a unique bridge between quantum measurement theory and fundamental physics tests.
